title: Crafting Reversible SFT Behaviors in Large Language Models
claim: A two-stage procedure first compresses a learned behavior into a sparse component, then a trigger input reverts it toward baseline.
layout: 2 dashed stage boxes, left-to-right, network diagrams with arrows and trigger inputs
description: A horizontal two-stage diagram. At far left is a blue base neural network. Arrows labeled 'Full SFT' and 'LCDD' lead through two networks inside the dashed Stage 1 box. The first is fully red, for the densely fine-tuned model. The second is mostly blue with a few red nodes, for the sparse carrier. Stage 2 sits in a second dashed box. An 'SFT-Eraser' arrow leads to a key icon and a trigger vector of orange circles. Two parallel rows follow. Without the trigger, green input nodes feed the carrier network with red nodes and produce a red 'SFT Behavior' box. With the trigger, the carrier's red nodes are crossed out with zigzag marks and produce a blue 'Base Behavior' box. Red marks the SFT-induced behavior and blue marks the base behavior. The eye starts at the left networks and follows the arrows to the two outcome boxes.
caption: An overview of the LCDD + SFT-Eraser pipeline. Stage 1: standard SFT distributes the induced behavior broadly across model parameters (red), followed by LCDD that compresses the SFT-induced behavior into a sparse carrier. Components outside the carrier are reduced to their base-model state by construction (blue). Stage 2: SFT-Eraser optimizes a soft trigger. Under normal inference without the trigger, the carrier preserves SFT behavior, while with the trigger, carrier activations are driven toward the base model.
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) induces new behaviors in large language models, yet imposes no structural constraint on how these behaviors are distributed within the model. Existing behavior interpretation methods, such as circuit attribution approaches, identify sparse subnetworks correlated with SFT-induced behaviors post-hoc. However, the fine-tuned model may still carry the behavior through other pathways, so such subnetworks offer no guaranteed handle for selectively controlling SFT-induced behaviors at inference time. We pursue a constructive alternative by asking: can an SFT-induced behavior be deliberately compressed into a sparse subnetwork, termed a *carrier*, that is sufficient for the behavior and, by construction, necessary for it, while remaining controllable at inference time without weight modification? We propose (a) **Loss-Constrained Dual Descent (LCDD)**, which constructs such carriers by jointly optimizing routing masks and model weights under an explicit utility budget, and (b) **SFT-Eraser**, a soft trigger prompt optimized via activation matching on extracted carrier channels, to revert the SFT-induced behavior toward the base model. Across safety, fixed-response, and style behaviors on four model families, LCDD yields sparse carriers that preserve target behaviors while enabling strong reversion when triggered by SFT-Eraser. Our ablation study shows that triggered LCDD models are consistently closer to the base model than identically triggered standard SFT models. The crafted structure is therefore what drives this reversion. These results establish training-time construction as a practical route to localizing and selectively suppressing SFT-induced behaviors in deployed models.
